newsitem.title: USA: Canada plans to start own satellite TV industry.
newsitem.headline: Canada plans to start own satellite TV industry.

text.p: Canada has signaled it plans to develop its own direct broadcast satellite (DBS) TV service rather than rely on the help of U.S. companies such as Tele-Communications Inc to jump-start the business.

The decision comes in response to a ruling by the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday to reject a bid by TCI and TelQuest Ventures to beam TV programs into the U.S. from two satellites in Canadian-authorized orbits. The satellites also would have beamed shows into Canada.

In a letter dated October 28 in anticipation of the FCC decision, Canada's minister of industry, John Manley, said he planed to "proceed forthwith" with an official call for applications to develop "Canadian DBS facilities using Canadian orbital and spectrum resources."

Manley's letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, was to the Canadian corporation Telesat Canada. TCI and TelQuest, both of which are based in Colorado, had planned to use two satellites that had not yet been licensed by the Canadian government and that would be owned and operated by Telesat Canada.
The FCC had rejected the TCI and TelQuest requests, saying the satellites the companies planned to use had not yet been licensed by the Canadian government.

At the heart of the dispute, however, is the Clinton administration's objection to allowing a Canadian satellite to beam programs into the United States without U.S. operators enjoying the same freedom to broadcast into Canada.

In his letter, Manley said that, unless the FCC granted the DBS applications by Friday, his government would withdraw its "support in principle" that could have enabled the TCI and TelQuest ventures to proceed.

TelQuest and TCI had argued in their petition to the FCC that the Canadian government had provided sufficient authorization for Telesat's proposed satellites in the form of the "support in principle" letter from Manley.

"It is unfortunate that this step is necessary, but with the absence of a decision on the U.S. side despite the efforts of you and your partners, we have to move to other avenues to provide satellite capacity," Manley told Telesat.
"I regret that the U.S. Administration did not share my support for this initiative as it would have been to the benefit of consumers in both countries.
"I believe that Canada and the U.S. should work toward an arrangement that would accommodate such innovative approaches in the future."
